links.note: 251 asks how one who eats another's flesh to enlarge his own (தன்னூன் பெருக்கற்கு) can exercise அருள்; 968 asks whether a life that nurses the flesh (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is any medicine once dignity is lost. Both use ஊன், one's own flesh, for a body tended at the cost of something higher: அருள் in one verse, honour in the other.

72 says the loveless keep everything for themselves, while the loving belong to others even in their bones (என்பும் உரியர் பிறர்க்கு). 251 describes the reverse movement: another's body (பிறிது ஊன்) taken to build one's own. Read together, the body is the measure in both: love gives it over, and the eater of flesh takes another's.

315 asks what understanding has achieved if one does not guard another's pain as one's own (பிறிதின்நோய் தந்நோய்போல்). 251 sets the same pair, self and other (தன் ஊன் / பிறிது ஊன்), the wrong way round: the other's flesh serves one's own. 315 gives the general test that 251's rhetorical question about அருள் applies to eating.

Both verses explain அருள் by putting it beside பொருள்: 247 says that world is not for those without அருள் just as this world is not for those without wealth, and 252 says holding அருள் (அருளாட்சி) is not for flesh-eaters just as holding wealth (பொருளாட்சி) is not for those who do not guard it. 252 takes the comparison one step on: அருள், like wealth, is something that can be lost through carelessness.

252 takes it as given that holding wealth is not for those who do not look after it (பொருளாட்சி போற்றாதார்க்கு இல்லை). 376 says what is not one's portion will not stay however anxiously it is guarded, and what is one's own will not leave even if carried out and poured away (பரியினும் ஆகாவாம் ... சொரியினும் போகா தம). The conflict holds if ஆட்சி is read as possession, as Manakkudavar and Pope read it; Parimelazhagar reads it as getting the benefit of wealth, which softens it.

253 says the mind of one who has eaten a creature's body with relish does not turn to good (நன்னூக்காது), like the heart of one holding a weapon. 285 says a loving nature with அருள் in view (அருள்கருதி) is not found in those who, with goods in view (பொருள்கருதி), watch for another's lapse. In both, what the mind is fixed on, flesh or another's property, leaves no room for அருள்; Parimelazhagar glosses 253 the same way, as a mind that looks only to the meat.

The two verses open with almost the same words. 321: if asked what virtuous action is, it is not killing, and killing brings every other kind of deed (அறவினை யாதெனின் கொல்லாமை கோறல்). 254, as Parimelazhagar construes it, defines அருள் and its opposite by the same pair, கொல்லாமை and கோறல், and then adds that eating that flesh is not பொருள். The chapter on meat borrows the non-killing chapter's definition and extends it from the killer to the eater. (The edition's text of 254 has lost its first letter; it should begin அருளல்லது.)

Both verses use பொருள் in an unusual, moral sense alongside அருள். 246 says those who leave அருள் and do what should not be done have left பொருள் and forgotten (பொருள்நீங்கிப் பொச்சாந்தார்); 254 calls eating flesh பொருளல்லது. Parimelazhagar takes பொருள் in 254 as virtue (so that பொருளல்லது is sin) and in 246 as the lasting good one should have done.

Both verses say where உயிர்நிலை, the standing or seat of life, lies. 80: it follows the way of love (அன்பின் வழியது உயிர்நிலை), and without love a body is bone wrapped in skin. 255: it lies in not eating flesh (உண்ணாமை உள்ளது உயிர்நிலை). Parimelazhagar takes the phrase in 255 to mean creatures' lives staying in their bodies; either way, both verses make life's hold on the body depend on a virtue.

255 says that if one eats flesh, அளறு (the mire, hell) will not open its mouth (அண்ணாத்தல் செய்யாது), which Parimelazhagar explains as not opening to let him out again. 835 says a fool can in one birth make the அளறு he will enter and sink in for seven (எழுமையும் தான் புக்கழுந்தும் அளறு). Both use the same rare word for a hell one makes for oneself and does not get out of.

326 says Death, the eater of life (உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று), does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing. 255 gives hell a mouth (அண்ணாத்தல்), which on Parimelazhagar's reading has swallowed the eater of flesh and will not open again. In both the language of eating is turned on the human: the one who spares life is not eaten, and the one who eats is.

329 says people whose work is killing (கொலைவினையர்) are of base occupation in the eyes of those who discern baseness. 256 argues that no one would supply flesh for a price (விலைப்பொருட்டால்) if the world did not kill, or on Manakkudavar's reading கொள்ளாது did not buy, for the sake of eating. 256 moves the blame that 329 puts on the slaughterer back to the eater whose demand creates the trade; Parimelazhagar says it answers the claim that the eater has no share in the killing.

1059 asks what distinction givers could have if there were none who wished to ask and receive (இரந்துகோள் மேவார் இலாஅக் கடை). 256 says none would bring flesh to sell if the world did not kill for eating. Both reason from a counterfactual about one party to the existence of the other: askers make givers possible, and eaters make sellers of flesh possible.

The two verses end with the same conditional: புண்ணது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (257) and வாளது உணர்வார்ப் பெறின் (334), 'if one could find people who perceive it as that'. 334 says what shows itself as a day is a blade sawing through life; 257 says meat is another creature's wound. In both the argument is a re-seeing of a familiar thing, and the phrasing admits that those who see it so are rare.

575 says that without kindly regard the eye is perceived as a wound (புண்ணென்று உணரப்படும்); 257 says flesh would not be eaten if people perceived it as another creature's wound (புண்ணது உணர்வார்). Both use புண் with உணர் to strip something of its usual standing, and both are about compassion: the eye without it is a sore, and food seen with it is a sore.

199: those of stainless vision, freed from delusion (மருள்தீர்ந்த மாசறு காட்சியவர்), do not say meaningless things even by a lapse. 258: those whose vision has parted from fault (செயிரின் தலைப்பிரிந்த காட்சியார்) do not eat flesh that has parted from life. The same figure, the person of clear காட்சி who simply does not do the thing, is used for speech and for food; restraint is presented as a consequence of seeing clearly, not of a rule.

174 says those of faultless vision who have conquered the senses (புலம்வென்ற புன்மையில் காட்சியவர்) will not covet, even thinking 'we have nothing'. 258 says those whose vision is free of fault do not eat flesh. Both attach an abstention that costs something, from another's goods or from meat, to காட்சி, and 174 adds the mastery of the senses that 258 leaves unstated.

259 says not taking a creature's life and eating it is better than pouring oblations in a thousand sacrifices (அவிசொரிந்து ஆயிரம் வேட்டலின்). 87 calls the tending of guests a வேள்வி and says its fruit is measured by the guest's worth. The Kural keeps the word for sacrifice while relocating its value: an ethical act is named as the sacrifice in 87 and ranked above the ritual in 259.

328 says that however great the gain said to bring good, gain that comes by killing is the lowest for the worthy (கொன்றாகும் ஆக்கங் கடை). Parimelazhagar takes this to be about killing in sacrifice for the gods, which householders are told brings great reward. On that reading it makes the same judgement as 259, which sets abstaining from one killing above a thousand sacrifices; the Tamil of 328 itself does not mention sacrifice.

295 says one who speaks truth in accord with his heart is above those who practise austerity together with giving (தவத்தொடு தானஞ்செய்வாரின் தலை). 259 says not killing one creature and eating it is better than a thousand sacrifices. Both rank a plain restraint, not lying and not killing, above the religious practices that carry the most prestige.

The two verses close with the same picture: எல்லா உயிருந் தொழும் (260) and மன்னுயிரெல்லாந் தொழும் (268), all living beings worship him. In 260 it is the one who does not kill and has refused flesh; in 268 it is the one who has fully gained his own life (தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான்), whom Parimelazhagar identifies with the doer of தவம். The neighbouring chapters give the same honour to non-killing and to austerity.

326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing; 260 says all living beings fold their hands (கைகூப்பி) and worship the one who does not kill and refuses flesh. Both state what the non-killer receives in return, and both put it as a response of life itself: living beings honour him, and the taker of life leaves him alone.

261 gives the form of தவம் as two things: bearing the pain that comes and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை). 984 says நோன்மை, austerity, has the goodness of not killing (கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை). A verse in the second book, written to define சால்பு, repeats the definition of austerity by its restraint toward other lives and not by its hardships.

261 calls bearing the pain that comes (உற்றநோய் நோன்றல்) the form of தவம்; Parimelazhagar takes the pain to be that of fasting and similar observances. 160 uses the same verb, நோல், to rank kinds of bearing: those who fast (உண்ணாது நோற்பார்) are great, but only after those who bear the harsh words of others. So within the endurance that 261 names, 160 puts the householder's patience under insult above the ascetic's fast.

157 says that though others do you wrong, it is good to feel the pain and not do what is contrary to virtue (நோநொந்து அறனல்ல செய்யாமை). 261 defines தவம் by the same two parts: bearing pain, and causing none to living beings. The chapter on forbearance asks of the householder, in dealings with those who wrong him, what 261 gives as the whole form of austerity.

262 says தவம் comes to those who already have தவம், and that for those without it taking it up is futile; Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar both read this as merit from earlier births. 273 pictures a person without strength (வலியில் நிலைமையான்) who takes on the form of the strong: a cow grazing in a tiger's skin. 273 shows what the futile undertaking of 262 looks like in practice. (The edition's text of 262 lacks the word அவம் at the start of the second line.)

373 says that however many subtle books one studies, the understanding that is truly one's own still prevails (தன் உண்மையறிவே மிகும்). 262 says austerity too succeeds only for those who already have it. Both hold that a discipline taken up now, study or austerity, yields only according to what the person brings to it; Parimelazhagar refers both to what earlier births have fixed.

262 says that for those without தவம், undertaking it is futile. 620 says those who toil on without flagging or delay will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்). If the தவம் one must already have is merit from former births, as Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar read it, then 262 makes present effort useless without a prior endowment, which is what 620 denies. On Kalaignar's reading, where it means present firmness and self-control, the conflict disappears.

42 names the householder as the support of those who have renounced (துறந்தார்க்கும் ... இல்வாழ்வான் என்பான் துணை), along with the destitute and the dead. 263 asks, with a wry கொல், whether the rest have forgotten தவம் out of a wish to provide for renouncers (துறந்தார்க்குத் துப்புரவு வேண்டி). It turns the duty stated in 42 into an explanation, or an excuse, for why householders do no austerity themselves.

263 speaks of the others, householders on Parimelazhagar's reading, as having forgotten தவம் while they provide for renouncers. 48 says a household life that keeps others on their way and does not slip from virtue has more endurance than those who do penance (நோற்பாரின் நோன்மை உடைத்து); Parimelazhagar reads 'keeps on their way' as supporting ascetics. On 48's account the provider has not forgotten austerity: his life already contains more of it.

1036 says that if ploughmen fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up desire' (விட்டேம் என்பார்) cannot keep their state. 263 assumes the same dependence: renouncers need others to supply their needs (துப்புரவு). Both verses note that renunciation rests on people who have not renounced.

261 says the form of தவம் is just this: bearing one's own pain and doing no harm to living beings (உயிர்க்குறுகண் செய்யாமை அற்றே). 264 says crushing foes (ஒன்னார்த் தெறல்) and raising friends come through தவம், if one so intends. Read plainly, austerity defined by harmlessness is credited three verses later with the power to destroy. Parimelazhagar eases this by taking the foes as enemies of virtue and by reading எண்ணின் as implying that ascetics do not normally think of such things.

899 says that if those of exalted resolve flare up (ஏந்திய கொள்கையார் சீறின்), even the king breaks midway and loses his rule. Parimelazhagar reads them as people of high vows, and Pope likewise. This is the power of 264, ஒன்னார்த் தெறல் through austerity, seen from the side of the king who must not provoke it.

29 says the anger of those who stand on the hill of good qualities cannot be withstood even for a moment (கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது), on Parimelazhagar's and Pope's reading; Kalaignar takes it to mean their anger does not last a moment. On the first reading it agrees with 264 that renouncers hold a power to ruin those who oppose them, though 264 makes it a matter of intention (எண்ணின்) and 29 of anger.

The two verses share a formula: வேண்டிய வேண்டியாங்கு எய்தலால் (265), what is wanted is obtained as it is wanted, and எண்ணிய எண்ணியாங்கு எய்துப (666), what is thought of is obtained as it was thought. 265 gives this as the reason austerity is striven for; 666 makes it depend on the planner's firmness (திண்ணியர் ஆகப் பெறின்). The promise made for austerity in the book of virtue is made for resolute action in the book of statecraft.

265 says austerity is practised because through it whatever is wanted is obtained as wanted. 362 says that if one must want, one should want not to be born, and that this comes by wanting not to want (வேண்டாமை வேண்ட வரும்). 362 narrows what the வேண்டிய of 265 should be; Parimelazhagar reads 265 itself as referring to results in the next life and release, while Manakkudavar takes it to include enjoyments.

309 says all one has thought of comes together at once if one never thinks of anger in the heart (உள்ளிய தெல்லாம் உடனெய்தும்). 265 says what is wanted is obtained as wanted through austerity. Both promise the fulfilment of wishes as the fruit of an inner discipline; Parimelazhagar reads 309 too as addressed to one doing தவம்.

266 says those who do தவம் are doing their own work (தங்கருமம்), and the rest, caught in desire, do what is futile (அவம்). 46 asks what one would gain by going off along the outside way if one conducts household life in the way of virtue (புறத்தாற்றில் போஒய்ப் பெறுவதெவன்). If the 'rest' of 266 means everyone who is not an ascetic, as Parimelazhagar's gloss of தவம் செய்வார் as renouncers suggests, the virtuous householder of 46 is among those doing futile work, and the verses disagree about whether his life is enough.

348 divides people the same way: those who have thoroughly renounced have reached the head, and the rest, confused, are caught in the net (மயங்கி வலைப்பட்டார் மற்றையவர்). 266 says those who do தவம் do their own work and the rest act in vain, caught in desire (ஆசையுட் பட்டு). Both use பட்டு / பட்டார், being caught, for everyone outside the ascetic's path; Parimelazhagar supplies 'the net of desire' in his gloss on 266.

267 says that for those able to endure, pain burning them makes them shine (ஒளிவிடும்), as gold shines the more it is heated. 630 says that if one takes what hurts as pleasure (இன்னாமை இன்பம் எனக்கொளின்), there comes a distinction even one's enemies admire. The ascetic's gain from pain in the first book has a worldly counterpart in the second: in both, pain borne in the right way adds to the person.

308 says that even if harm is done to you like the touch of massed flames (இணர்எரி தோய்வன்ன), not being angry is good if one can manage it. 267 says pain that burns (துன்பஞ் சுடச்சுட) makes those who can endure it shine like gold in fire. Both picture suffering as fire applied to a person; 308 asks only that it be borne without anger, and 267 says what the bearing produces.

346 says one who cuts off the pride of 'I' and 'mine' (யான் எனது என்னும் செருக்கு) enters a world above the gods'. 268 says all other beings worship the one who தன்னுயிர் தான் அறப் பெற்றான். Manakkudavar takes அற as 'ceasing': one in whom the notion that his life is himself has ended, and Kalaignar reads it similarly, which makes the verse the same claim as 346. Parimelazhagar instead reads it as fully possessing one's own life, where the agreement is weaker.

326 says Death, the eater of life, does not advance on the days of one who lives by not killing (செல்லாது உயிருண்ணுங் கூற்று). 269 says even leaping past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) becomes possible for those who have attained the power of austerity. Since 261 and 984 make non-killing the core of austerity, the two verses give the same exemption from கூற்று to what is largely the same practice.

620 says those who toil on without flagging will see the back even of fate (ஊழையும் உப்பக்கம் காண்பர்); 269 says even getting past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்) is within reach of those with the power of austerity. Each uses the particle உம், 'even', to name the one thing thought unbeatable and then says sustained effort beats it: labour in the book of statecraft, austerity in the book of virtue. (The edition's text of 269 ends with a stray letter, தலைப்பட்டவர்க்குல்.)

842 says that when a person without understanding gives gladly, the cause is nothing other than the receiver's தவம் (பெறுவான் தவம்). 270 says the have-nots are many because those who practise austerity are few. Both explain who gets and who lacks by austerity, and 842 shows the idea used in passing in the second book, as an accepted explanation.

616 says effort creates prosperity and the absence of effort brings in want (முயற்றின்மை இன்மை புகுத்தி விடும்). 270 says the have-nots (இலர்) are many because few practise austerity (நோற்பார் சிலர்). Both trace poverty to something people fail to do, but they name different things: present exertion in the chapter on labour, and austerity here, which the commentators take to bear fruit across births.
